analogy.p: Think of each parent as holding a pair of cards for one gene: a Bb parent holds a B card and a b card. To make a gamete, the parent hands over just one card, picked at random and face down, so half the time it is B and half the time it is b. Fertilisation is two cards, one from each parent, being laid side by side to make the child's pair. A Punnett square just lists every pair that could be laid down. The analogy breaks down because real alleles are stretches of DNA copied by meiosis rather than physical cards, and some real characteristics depend on many genes and the environment, so a two-card model cannot capture everything.

bullets: A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for a particular protein; it is found at a specific position (locus) on a chromosome.
Different forms of the same gene are called **alleles**.
The alleles are made of the same type of DNA but have slightly different base sequences, so they can code for slightly different proteins.
An individual normally has **two alleles** for each gene, one inherited from each parent.
Alleles are written using a letter: capital for dominant (B), lower case for recessive (b), using the same letter.
Only a few characteristics are controlled by a single gene; the rest involve many genes (see later).
Link: the alleles present operate at a molecular level (making different proteins) to produce a characteristic.
core.p: Some characteristics are controlled by a **single gene**, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans. A gene can exist in different forms, and these different forms of the same gene are called **alleles**. For instance a gene for fur colour might have an allele for brown fur and an allele for white fur. Which alleles an organism has decides which version of the characteristic it develops, so alleles are the reason individuals of the same species show variation.

bullets: Humans have **23 pairs of chromosomes**; 22 pairs are autosomes and one pair is the sex chromosomes.
One chromosome in each pair comes from the **mother** (egg) and one from the **father** (sperm).
The two chromosomes of a pair carry the **same genes** at the same positions.
This is why each person has two alleles of each gene.
The alleles on the two chromosomes may be identical or different.
Gametes (sex cells) have **only one** chromosome from each pair (23 in total), so they carry one allele of each gene.
Fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes (46) and the pairs.
core.p: Body cells contain chromosomes in **pairs**. In humans there are 23 pairs, 46 chromosomes in total, with one chromosome of each pair inherited from the mother and one from the father. The two chromosomes in a pair carry the same genes in the same order, so for any gene there are two copies, which may be the same allele or different alleles. Of the 23 pairs, 22 are autosomes and one pair is the sex chromosomes.

bullets: **Dominant allele** = always expressed (shown in the phenotype), even if only one copy is present; represented by a **capital letter** (B).
**Recessive allele** = only expressed if **two copies** are present (no dominant allele present); represented by the **lower case** of the same letter (b).
Use the same letter for both alleles in a cross, so that capital and lower case clearly belong to the same gene.
'Dominant' does not mean more common or better; it only describes how the allele is expressed.
A recessive characteristic can skip a generation, because it is hidden in heterozygous individuals.
Always state which allele is dominant before drawing the cross (a key: B = brown, b = white).
Exam wording: 'The allele for brown fur is dominant to the allele for white fur.'
core.p: The two alleles in a pair may not have equal influence. A **dominant allele** is always expressed, even if only one copy is present. A **recessive allele** is only expressed if two copies are present (that is, when no dominant allele is present). This is why two parents who both show the dominant characteristic can still have a child showing the recessive characteristic: each can carry a hidden recessive allele.

bullets: **Genotype** = the alleles an individual has (e.g. Bb).
**Phenotype** = the observable characteristic that is expressed (e.g. brown fur).
BB and Bb are different genotypes with the **same phenotype** (dominant).
A recessive phenotype can only be produced by the genotype bb.
Phenotype can also be affected by the environment (for example diet affecting height).
To work out an unknown genotype, start from the phenotype: a recessive phenotype is always homozygous recessive.
Exam tip: never mix up the two words; genotype = letters, phenotype = description.
core.p: The **genotype** is the combination of alleles that an individual has for a gene, written as letters (BB, Bb or bb). The **phenotype** is the characteristic that is actually expressed, such as brown fur or white fur. The alleles present, or genotype, operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that are expressed as the phenotype. Different genotypes can give the same phenotype (BB and Bb both show the dominant phenotype), but one phenotype corresponds to only one genotype if it is the recessive phenotype (bb).

bullets: **Homozygous** = two **identical** alleles (BB or bb).
**Heterozygous** = two **different** alleles (Bb).
**Homozygous dominant** = BB; **homozygous recessive** = bb.
Think: 'homo' = same, 'hetero' = different.
A **carrier** has one copy of a recessive allele for a disorder but does not have the disorder because the dominant allele is expressed.
Only homozygous recessive individuals (bb) show a recessive characteristic.
Homozygous dominant and heterozygous individuals look identical, so crosses may be needed to tell them apart.
core.p: The words homozygous and heterozygous describe whether the two alleles of a gene are the same or different. An individual with two identical alleles (BB or bb) is **homozygous**; one with two different alleles (Bb) is **heterozygous**. Homozygous individuals can be homozygous dominant (BB) or homozygous recessive (bb). A heterozygous individual shows the dominant phenotype but carries a recessive allele it can pass on; for inherited disorders such a person is called a **carrier**.

bullets: Gametes are **haploid**: they have half the normal number of chromosomes (23 in humans).
Each gamete contains **one allele** for each gene.
A **Bb** parent produces **B gametes and b gametes** in equal numbers (50:50).
A **BB** parent produces only B gametes; a **bb** parent only b gametes.
Gametes are produced by **meiosis**, which separates the chromosome pairs.
Gametes are produced randomly, so which allele any one gamete gets is a matter of chance.
In the genetic diagram, gametes are written as single letters, in circles if you wish.
core.p: Gametes (egg and sperm in animals) are made by cell division called **meiosis**. During meiosis the chromosome pairs are separated, so each gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair and therefore only one allele of each gene. A parent with genotype Bb therefore makes two types of gamete: half carry B and half carry b. A homozygous parent (BB or bb) can only make one type of gamete. Working out the gametes correctly is the first step in every genetic cross.

bullets: Fertilisation restores the **diploid** number of chromosomes.
Each parent gives one allele for each gene, so offspring have two alleles.
**Random fertilisation** means every gamete combination is equally likely.
The first offspring does not affect the next: each fertilisation is an independent event.
The cross Bb x Bb has 4 equally likely combinations: BB, Bb, Bb, bb.
Fertilisation is the reason that offspring show a mixture of both parents' characteristics.
Link: random fertilisation, along with meiosis, is a source of genetic variation.
core.p: When a sperm fuses with an egg at **fertilisation**, the two sets of alleles combine to form a zygote with a full set of chromosome pairs. Which sperm fertilises which egg is **random**, so every possible combination of gametes is equally likely. This randomness is why we can only talk about **probabilities** in genetics, not certainties. The Punnett square is simply a table that lists all the possible combinations of the gametes.

bullets: Step 1: write a **key** (e.g. B = brown fur (dominant), b = white fur (recessive)).
Step 2: write the **genotypes of the parents** (e.g. Bb x Bb).
Step 3: work out the **gametes** each parent can produce (one allele from each).
Step 4: draw a 2 x 2 grid and write one parent's gametes along the top and the other down the side.
Step 5: fill in each box by combining the letter above and the letter at the side; write the **dominant (capital) allele first** (Bb, never bB).
Step 6: write the **genotypes** and then the **phenotypes** of the offspring.
Step 7: state the answer as a **ratio, fraction or percentage** and answer the actual question.
Check: a monohybrid Punnett square has four boxes, so each box is a probability of 1 in 4 (25%).
core.h: How to draw a Punnett square (method)
core.p: A **Punnett square** (genetic cross diagram) is a method for predicting the results of a monohybrid cross, a cross involving one gene. Follow the same steps every time, and write each step clearly because examiners give marks for the key, the parents' genotypes, the gametes, the completed square and the final answer. A correct layout also stops you making small mistakes with alleles.

bullets: Count boxes: 4 boxes in total, so each box = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.
Bb x Bb: genotype ratio **1 : 2 : 1** (BB : Bb : bb); phenotype ratio **3 : 1** (dominant : recessive).
Probability of a recessive offspring from Bb x Bb = 1/4 = 25%.
Expected number = probability x total offspring (e.g. 25% of 80 = 20).
Simplify ratios if possible (2 : 2 becomes 1 : 1).
A ratio is not the same as a fraction: 3 : 1 means 3/4 and 1/4 of the total.
Give the units/format asked for: 'as a percentage', 'as a ratio' or 'the probability'.
core.h: Reading the results: ratios, fractions and percentages
core.p: Each box in a 2 x 2 square represents an equally likely outcome. Counting boxes gives you a ratio, and the ratio can be converted to a probability or percentage. For Bb x Bb the genotype ratio is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb and the phenotype ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive. Probabilities can be written as a fraction (1/4), a decimal (0.25) or a percentage (25%). You may be asked how many offspring of a given number are expected to show a certain phenotype.

bullets: **BB x bb**: all offspring **Bb**; all show the dominant phenotype.
**Bb x Bb**: 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb; phenotypes **3 dominant : 1 recessive** (75% : 25%).
**Bb x bb**: 1 Bb : 1 bb; phenotypes **1 dominant : 1 recessive** (50% : 50%).
**BB x Bb**: 1 BB : 1 Bb; all show the dominant phenotype.
**bb x bb**: all bb; all show the recessive phenotype.
**BB x BB**: all BB.
If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, both parents must carry at least one recessive allele.
core.h: Key crosses you should be able to do
core.p: There are only a few combinations of parental genotypes, and it saves time to know the results. Every possible cross can be worked out from a Punnett square, but if you recognise the pattern you can check your answer quickly. The most important ones are Bb x Bb (3:1), Bb x bb (1:1) and BB x bb (all Bb). Remember that if either parent is homozygous dominant (BB) all offspring show the dominant phenotype.

bullets: The ratio predicts the **likelihood**, not the exact number in a family.
In a family of 4 from Bb x Bb you do not have to get exactly 3 dominant and 1 recessive.
**Large samples** give results closer to the expected ratio (e.g. 400 mice).
Each fertilisation is **independent**: previous outcomes do not change the probability.
'Gambler's fallacy' mistake: saying the next child is more likely to be recessive because the earlier ones were not.
The probability that two specific independent events both happen is found by multiplying (1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16).
Use the word 'chance' or 'probability', never 'will definitely'.
core.p: A Punnett square gives the **theoretical probability**, the chance of each outcome, not a guarantee of what happens. Because fertilisation is random, the results from a small number of offspring can differ a lot from the ratio. For example, two Bb parents could have three brown offspring in a row. Only with large numbers of offspring do the observed results get close to the expected 3 : 1 ratio. Each offspring is independent, so the chance that the next child has the recessive phenotype is always 1 in 4, whatever the earlier children were like.

bullets: A **recessive-phenotype individual is always bb**.
Two parents without a trait who have an affected child: the trait is **recessive** and both parents are **carriers (Bb)**.
Offspring ratio ~**3 : 1** -> both parents Bb.
Offspring ratio ~**1 : 1** -> one parent Bb, the other bb.
**All** offspring dominant from a dominant x recessive cross -> the dominant parent is likely BB.
In a family tree, circles are usually females and squares males; shaded shapes show the characteristic.
Fill in what you know for certain first (all bb), then work out the others.
Check any answer by drawing a Punnett square for the parents you have decided on.
core.h: Working backwards: finding parental genotypes and using family trees
core.p: Exam questions often give you the offspring and ask for the parents' genotypes. The key is to start with the recessive phenotype, because it must be bb, and one b must come from each parent. If two parents with the dominant phenotype have a child with the recessive phenotype, both parents must be heterozygous (Bb). If the offspring ratio is about 1 : 1, one parent is Bb and the other is bb; if all offspring show the dominant phenotype the parent could be BB. In a family tree (pedigree) the same reasoning is applied to each generation.

bullets: Many characteristics are controlled by **several genes interacting**.
Such characteristics show **continuous variation** (a range of values) not clear-cut categories.
The environment also affects phenotype (for example a plant grown in the dark or a person's weight).
A Punnett square only works for a characteristic controlled by one gene with a dominant and recessive allele.
Single-gene examples: fur colour in mice, red-green colour blindness in humans, and inherited disorders such as polydactyly and cystic fibrosis.
Higher tier: be ready to explain why a Punnett square is a model that has limits.
core.h: Most characteristics involve many genes (and the environment)
core.p: Single-gene inheritance is only the simplest case. **Most characteristics are the result of multiple genes interacting**, rather than a single gene. Examples are height, skin colour and many body features, which have a continuous range of values rather than two clear categories. These characteristics are also affected by the environment (nutrition, exercise, sunlight). Punnett squares for a single gene therefore cannot fully predict such characteristics.

bullets: Females have **XX**; males have **XY**.
All eggs carry an X chromosome; **sperm carry X or Y**.
The cross XX x XY gives **XX : XY = 1 : 1**, so 50% girls and 50% boys.
This is a probability for each child, not a guarantee of equal numbers in a family.
The Y chromosome carries the gene that causes testes to develop.
Detail of the inherited disorders and sex determination is in the next topic.
core.h: Sex determination as an inheritance example
core.p: Human sex is determined by one pair of chromosomes, the sex chromosomes. Females are **XX** and males are **XY**. All eggs carry an X chromosome, but sperm carry either an X or a Y, so it is the father's sperm that decides the sex of a baby. A Punnett square for XX x XY shows an equal chance (50%, 1 in 2) of a boy or a girl at each pregnancy. The Punnett method is exactly the same as for alleles of a gene.

bullets: **Meiosis**: gametes carry one allele of each gene; fertilisation restores pairs.
**Protein synthesis**: different alleles have different base sequences and so code for different proteins.
**Inherited disorders**: polydactyly (caused by a dominant allele) and cystic fibrosis (caused by a recessive allele) are predicted with the same Punnett squares.
**Evolution**: advantageous alleles are more likely to be passed on.
**Selective breeding**: breeders choose parents that carry the desired alleles over many generations.
**Ethics**: embryo screening for alleles raises ethical issues (you may need to evaluate these).
Maths skills: ratios, fractions, percentages, probability (e.g. 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16).
core.h: Links to other topics and exam skills
core.p: This topic connects strongly to others. Genotypes and phenotypes link to protein synthesis (alleles code for different proteins), meiosis explains why gametes carry one allele, inherited disorders use the same cross diagrams, and natural selection depends on the alleles passed to the next generation. Selective breeding relies on choosing parents with desired alleles. Mendel, a monk working with pea plants, first showed that characteristics were inherited as separate units (later called genes); his work was not appreciated until after his death.

exam: Command words: **state** = one fact; **explain** = give a reason; **complete/draw** a Punnett square = fill in all boxes; **calculate** probability or percentage = show working.
Always include a **key** saying which letter is dominant and which is recessive; the allele letters must be the same letter in capital and lower case.
Marks for a cross are typically: parents' genotypes (1), gametes (1), correct offspring genotypes in the square (1), correct phenotypes/ratio or probability (1).
Write the gametes as single letters, one allele per gamete, and make sure each box is a combination of one letter from each parent.
For 'predict the probability' give a fraction, ratio or percentage as asked, e.g. '1 in 4, 25%, 0.25'.
For 'explain why two parents without the condition had an affected child': both parents are heterozygous carriers (Bb), each passes on a recessive allele, the child is bb, the chance is 1 in 4.
For 'expected numbers' questions multiply the probability by the total (e.g. 1/4 x 80 = 20); say that actual results may differ because fertilisation is random.
Define key terms with exam wording: dominant (always expressed even if only one copy), recessive (only expressed if two copies present).
Do not describe the Punnett square as 'proving' or 'guaranteeing' the outcome; use 'chance' or 'probability'.
Show family-tree reasoning: start with the recessive phenotype (bb), then fill in the parents, then check with a Punnett square.
Check the question wording for the tier: this content is for both tiers, but Higher questions may use unfamiliar contexts or ask you to evaluate the model.

mistakes.r: A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
mistakes.w: Dominant means it is the most common allele or the strongest.

mistakes.r: A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.
Genotype is the alleles (e.g. Bb); phenotype is the characteristic expressed (e.g. brown fur).
Each gamete carries only one allele, so a Bb parent has gametes B and b.
mistakes.w: Putting both of a parent's alleles in one gamete (e.g. gametes Bb).

mistakes.r: Use the same letter in capital and lower case, with a key.
mistakes.w: Using different letters for the two alleles (e.g. B and R).

mistakes.r: It is a probability; actual results can differ, especially for small numbers.
mistakes.w: Saying a 3 : 1 ratio means exactly 3 out of every 4 children.

mistakes.r: Each fertilisation is independent, so the chance stays 1 in 4 (or whatever the cross predicts).
mistakes.w: Thinking the next child is more likely to be recessive after several dominant ones.

mistakes.r: Give the answer in the form asked: 25% or 1/4 or 0.25.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer as '3 : 1' when asked for a percentage or probability.

mistakes.r: Write the capital letter first, Bb.
mistakes.w: Writing bB in the offspring boxes.

summary: You must understand how a single gene with two alleles is inherited: the terms dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype and phenotype, and how to build and read a Punnett square (genetic cross diagram) to predict the probability and ratio of offspring outcomes. It matters because this is a standard multi-mark exam skill, and it explains how characteristics, and many inherited conditions, are passed from parents to children.

terms.d: A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
A different form of the same gene.
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present (no dominant allele present).
The combination of alleles that an individual has for a gene.
The characteristics that are expressed from the genotype (what the organism looks like or does).
Having two identical alleles for a gene (e.g. BB or bb).
Having two different alleles for a gene (e.g. Bb).
A sex cell (egg or sperm) with half the normal number of chromosomes, containing one allele for each gene.
A structure in the nucleus made of a long molecule of DNA carrying many genes; they occur in pairs in body cells.
The fusion of a male and a female gamete to form a zygote with the full number of chromosomes.
A genetic cross that looks at the inheritance of one characteristic controlled by a single gene.
A diagram (genetic cross diagram) used to predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring and their probabilities.
A person who has one copy of a recessive allele for a disorder but does not show the disorder.
A measure of the chance that an outcome will happen; for example 1 in 4, 0.25 or 25%.
The pair of chromosomes that determine sex: XX in females and XY in males.
A comparison of numbers, such as 3 : 1, showing the expected proportions of outcomes.

worked.ans: (a) BB, Bb, Bb, bb. (b) 3 brown : 1 white. (c) 2 white (expected, but the actual number could differ because fertilisation is random).
worked.q: In mice, brown fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). Two heterozygous brown mice are crossed. (a) Draw a Punnett square. (b) State the ratio of brown to white offspring. (c) The mice have 8 offspring; how many are expected to be white? [5 marks]
steps: Key: B = brown (dominant), b = white (recessive). Parents Bb x Bb.
Gametes: B or b from each parent.
Phenotypes: BB, Bb, Bb brown (3); bb white (1) -> ratio 3 : 1.

worked.ans: The brown parent is heterozygous (Bb). Some offspring are white (bb), so they must have inherited a recessive allele from each parent; so the brown parent has a recessive allele as well as the dominant one. The 1 : 1 ratio matches Bb x bb.
worked.q: A brown mouse (B dominant) of unknown genotype is crossed with a white mouse. The litter is 6 brown and 6 white. What is the genotype of the brown parent? Explain your answer. [3 marks]
steps: White mouse is recessive so must be bb.
The 6 white offspring are bb, so each received a b from the brown parent.
So the brown parent must carry a recessive allele: it is Bb.
Check: Bb x bb gives 1 Bb : 1 bb = 50% brown : 50% white, matching the 1 : 1 ratio.

worked.ans: Both parents are heterozygous (Bb); the white baby is homozygous recessive (bb), having received a recessive allele from each parent. The recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present. The probability that the next baby is white is 1/4 (25%).
worked.q: Two brown mice (B dominant) have a white baby. Explain how this is possible and give the probability that their next baby is also white. [4 marks]
steps: The white baby is bb, so it inherited one b allele from each parent.
So each brown parent has a b allele hidden by the dominant B allele: both are Bb (carriers).
Bb x Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb so probability of bb = 1/4.
Each fertilisation is independent, so the answer is the same as for the first baby.
